questions.text: Step 1 says the API reads the in-memory routing config and step 8 says instances poll every 10 seconds. Which process or thread does the polling, and does a request ever wait on it?
questions.about: 1. Receive the request and route / 8. Deliver the active pointer without a redeploy

questions.text: What does 'inference' actually run on in the API process (CPU, GPU, a library, a separate model server)? And what exactly are 'scored items' before 'removes duplicates and filters'?

Step 2 says the record carries features for every in-flight model, and step 6 writes the union of active, previous and shadow features. How does the active model pick out only its own features from the record?
What is the 'popular list' and how is it computed in the daily job? Is it the same for every user?
In step 5, what does the 'background sender' run as, and what is the 'message queue' (which product, who consumes it)? How do shadow workers get deployed and who runs them?
questions.about: 5. Hand off to shadow, after the response

questions.text: The promotion tool, rollback tool and evaluation job are named but not described. Are they a CLI, a service, a person clicking something? Who runs them and how do they authenticate to write the routing config?
questions.about: 9. Start shadow for a candidate / 12. Promotion gate

questions.text: Step 6 says the previous version's features stay in the job and step 14 says rollback needs them. When a new promotion happens, how do the old 'previous' features get dropped, and when is it safe to?
Step 10 says shadow checks record age at the 'time of the original request'. What timestamp is used for that, and what is feature_age in the results?
What does 'Days in shadow: at least 7' count, given the clock starts at the first shadow result and shadow could be switched off or restarted in between?
questions.about: 11. Compare results and build the gate report

questions.text: Step 12 requires the ML lead's approval against a specific report, but reports are regenerated hourly and must be under 24 hours old. How does the approver approve a report that will be replaced? What happens when a new one arrives?

answers.text: Each instance runs the poll on its own background thread. A request only reads the in-memory copy and never waits on the poll, so a slow registry cannot add latency.

The brief does not name the runtime. I assumed the model runs in-process in the API (step 10 says shadow uses the same inference code). Scored items are candidate item IDs with a model score, best first. The exact filter rules are not defined; added to open items.
Each registry version lists its required feature names. The model reads those names from the record's features and ignores the others. Added one line to step 3.
The brief says only that a popular-items list is recomputed daily. It is one global list, the same for every user. How popularity is scored is not specified; added to open items.

The sender is a background thread in the API process. The queue product, who deploys the shadow workers and who runs them are not specified in the brief; added to open items. Workers are a separate service that consumes the queue.

They are command-line tools run by people (the evaluation job is scheduled). Only these hold write access to the routing config, and each write records its author. The exact authentication method is not specified and is left to the platform team. Added to the assumptions.

The job rebuilds the union from the current routing config at every run. After a promotion the old previous version is no longer a rollback target, so its extra features drop out at the next run. This is safe because the new previous is the old active. Added to step 6.
Age is the message's request time minus the record's materialized_at. feature_age in the results is that same value. I added request time to the step 5 message and defined the age in step 10.

The clock counts continuous time in shadow from the first result. Any switch-off or restart resets it to zero. This is the simplest safe reading of at least 7 days. Whether a request minimum is needed stays an open item.

The approver approves the report they saw, recorded by report ID. That approval counts for 24 hours from that report, and the promotion tool also requires the latest report to pass the numbers. After the 24 hours, or if a new report fails, the ML lead approves again. Changed step 12 from exact report to this rule.

questions.text: Step 3 says inference is in-process, but what exactly is the 'model' object loaded from the registry (a file format, a library)? Does the API process need to understand it, and how does it run one request's scoring with the 125 ms deadline enforced?
Where do the 'candidate item IDs' come from that the model scores? Does the model score the whole catalogue, or is there an earlier retrieval step the document does not show?

Step 2 says an instance cannot take traffic if the config cannot be read, and step 8 says it keeps its last config. At cold start, must it also have loaded the active model before it is ready? What does 'ready' check?

In step 5, the message carries the whole feature record and 20 items. How many requests per second are in shadow, and how does a message reach the queue from the background sender (batching, one by one)? What does 'disabled automatically if the drop rate stays high' do, and who writes that change?
questions.about: 5. Hand off to shadow, after the response

questions.text: Step 14 says a promotion writes previous = old active and shadow = null. Does the shadow candidate being promoted keep its 7-day report afterwards, and what happens to messages still in the shadow queue for the old candidate?
questions.about: 14. Switch the active version, and roll back

questions.text: Step 11 computes error rate from shadow results. How does it avoid mixing in results from an earlier shadow run of the same version, given the clock resets on restart?
questions.about: 11. Compare results and build the gate report

questions.text: Step 8 says an instance loads a version it does not hold when active or previous changes. How long does a load take and how does it keep serving while loading? Also when does an instance drop an old version from memory?
questions.about: 8. Deliver the active pointer without a redeploy

answers.text: The brief names no artifact format or inference runtime, so I cannot say what the model object is. I added a line to step 3 that the API checks remaining time before and after inference and treats a missed deadline as a failure, and listed format and runtime under open item 8.
The brief does not say whether the model scores the whole catalogue or sits behind a retrieval step. I treat it as part of what the model artifact does. Added a line in step 3 and to open item 8.
Yes. An instance is ready only when it has read the routing config and loaded the active and previous models. Otherwise it takes no traffic, so a request never waits on a cold load. Added to step 1.

The brief gives no request rate. Shadow volume is 10% of non-fallback requests; I added that to step 5 and listed the rate as an open item. The sender ships in small batches. I removed the automatic disable on high drop rate, since nothing was defined to write that change. A high drop rate now raises an alert and the on-call uses the kill switch.

Yes, reports stay attached to the version in the registry. A worker reads the current routing config for each message, and discards the message if shadow is null, so leftover messages after promotion or kill switch are ignored. Added to steps 10 and 11.

Each shadow start gets a new salt, which doubles as the run ID. Results rows carry shadow_salt, and the evaluation job counts only rows matching the current run's salt. Added to the routing config note and steps 9 to 11.

Real load time is not known; it stays open item 5. Loading runs on the instance's background thread while requests keep using the current model, and the pointer swaps only after the load succeeds. An instance keeps exactly active and previous, and drops other versions once no in-flight request holds them. Added to step 8.

questions.text: In step 3 the API 'removes duplicates and filters' scored items. If after filtering fewer than 20 items remain, what does the response contain, and is that a fallback or a normal response?

Step 8 says an instance must hold both active and previous in memory. Step 12 promotes a candidate that was only run in shadow workers. When promotion writes active=candidate, does each instance load it only after the write (so there is a delay), or is it loaded earlier? What do requests use during that time?
questions.about: 8. Deliver the active pointer without a redeploy / 14. Switch the active version

questions.text: What exactly is the 'kill switch' in step 10 and step 5: is it a separate command, or the promotion tool setting shadow to null? Who may run it, and how does it differ from the three writers named in the assumptions?
In step 14, how does the tool know 'nearly all instances report the new version'? Where do instances report it, and what does the tool do if a few never report?
questions.about: 14. Switch the active version, and roll back

questions.text: Step 9 says the promotion tool checks that the materialization job config was updated and has run. Who updates that job config to add the candidate's features, and how does the job learn them: from the routing config's shadow candidate only after shadow starts?
questions.about: 9. Start shadow for a candidate / 6. Hourly materialization

questions.text: The step 2 timeout is 30 ms and the response 'reason' lists timeout. When inference misses its 125 ms deadline, is reason also 'timeout' or 'inference_error'? And does the fallback response still meet the 150 ms total?

In step 5, how does the API know the response 'came from step 3' and the user is in shadow bucket, when a deployment has a candidate whose features the record might lack for only some users? Does the API check candidate features before enqueueing, or leave it to the worker?
questions.about: 5. Hand off to shadow, after the response

answers.text: The API tops the list up from the popular list (skipping duplicates) so the response always has 20, as the brief requires. It stays a normal response with fallback false, and the topped-up count is counted. If nothing remains after filtering, it counts as an inference failure and goes to fallback. Exact filter rules remain an open item.

Instances do not preload a shadow candidate, because only shadow workers run candidates. Each instance loads the new version in the background after the promotion write. Until its load finishes, its requests keep using the old active version. The switch therefore takes up to one poll interval plus load time, and I accept that delay. Rollback is unaffected because previous is already resident. Added to steps 8 and 14.

The kill switch is the promotion tool's stop-shadow command, which sets shadow to null. It is not a fourth writer. The ML engineer or the on-call engineer may run it, and it writes the routing config like the other two tools, with the author recorded. Defined in the assumptions and step 10.

Each instance reports its loaded version in its health metrics (step 8), and the tool reads those. Promotion is complete when every ready instance reports the new version. An instance that has not reported after 5 minutes is listed and a human decides to fix the artifact or roll back. The tool takes no automatic action. Which metrics system holds this is not specified and is added to open item 8.

You found a real gap. As written, the job only learned the candidate's features after shadow started, but the pre-check needed them before. Fix: starting shadow has two phases. Phase 1 writes shadow with percent 0 and a salt. No user is bucketed in, but the job's union already includes the candidate, because it rebuilds the union from the routing config every run. After the job has run, phase 2 checks the features and sets percent 10. No separate job config exists. Changed steps 6 and 9 and the routing config note.

The reason timeout means only the 30 ms feature lookup. A missed 125 ms inference deadline is inference_error. The fallback still meets 150 ms because it does no network I/O and the inference deadline leaves 25 ms. Added to step 4.

The API does not check candidate features before enqueueing. It only checks the bucket and that the response came from step 3. The worker checks the snapshot against the candidate's required features and records a skip with reason missing_feature or stale. This keeps the request thread free of shadow logic. Added to step 5.

questions.text: Step 1 says a request takes a reference to the active model, and step 8 says the pointer swaps after load. When shadow's candidate is in the routing config at percent 10, does the API process itself ever need the candidate's artifact, or only its required-feature list?

Step 12 requires 'the required features are still present in the store (re-checked now)'. How does the tool check this: by sampling records, scanning all users, or reading something else? And what counts as 'present' if some users lack a feature?

Step 9 phase 2 says the tool reports 'the share of users whose records contain all the candidate's features' but then 'refuses unless every required feature exists in the online store'. Are these the same check? Does phase 2 proceed if only 90% of users have the features?

In step 14, promotion writes shadow = null and active = candidate. What does the materialization job do for the candidate's features between that write and the instances finishing their load? Is anything at risk if the job runs in that window?
questions.about: 14. Switch the active version, and roll back

questions.text: In step 3 a version can be active on one instance and a new one on another for a short time. If an instance is on the old active but the new record lacks a feature the old version needs, what happens? Is that covered by the union rule in step 6?

Step 11 says the 7-day clock starts at the first shadow result. Where does the evaluation job read that time from, and how does it detect an 'interruption' during the 7 days (for example a gap in results or a shadow switch-off)?
questions.about: 11. Compare results and build the gate report

questions.text: How does a shadow worker run the candidate when it needs to load it? Which process loads the candidate artifact in the workers, and does it learn of a new candidate by reading the routing config per message?

answers.text: No. The API never loads or runs the candidate, and it does not even need the candidate's required-feature list. From the shadow entry it needs only percent and salt for bucketing. The worker holds the artifact and checks features. Added a line to step 1.

The tool samples random user records from the online store and reports, per required feature, the share of records that have it. 'Present' means the feature appears in the sample. A feature absent from every sampled record blocks the step. A partial share does not block, because workers skip users lacking a feature and the skip rate is gated separately (open item 4). The sample size is not decided; added as open item 8. Defined once in step 9 and referenced from step 12.

They were two different checks and that was confusing. Now it is one check, run in both phases and in step 12. Phase 2 proceeds if every feature appears in the sample, even when only 90% of users have it. The share is reported, and the effect of partial coverage shows up as a skip rate in the gate report, which open item 4 asks someone to threshold.

Nothing is at risk. The union in step 6 is rebuilt from the routing config each run. After the promotion write, the new active version is in the union as active, and the old active is in it as previous. So instances on either version find their features. Added a line to steps 6 and 14.

Yes, the union covers it. During a switch the old active becomes previous, and previous is in the union, so the old version's features stay materialized. If a record still lacks a needed feature, step 2 returns a missing_feature fallback for that request. One edge case remains: an instance stuck two promotions behind would lose its features after the next run. I did not add handling, since a stuck instance is already listed for a human in step 14.

You found a real gap: the clock was tied to the first result, which the evaluation job cannot reliably find. Now the promotion tool records the write time of the percent-10 start in the registry, and that is the run start. Days in shadow is now minus that start while shadow still holds that run's salt. Any switch-off or restart ends the run (new salt, new start), so no separate gap detection is needed. Result gaps show as loss and low sample count. Changed steps 9 and 11 and open item 3.

Each worker process reads the routing config per message (cached a few seconds), and if it does not hold the candidate it loads it from the registry on demand, keeping one candidate resident at a time. Messages wait in the queue during the load. Load time is not known (open item 5). Added to step 10.

questions.text: After a rollback sets `active` back to `previous`, what does `previous` hold? Does it stay the same (the bad version), become empty, or something else? Which version's features does the materialization union then keep?
questions.about: 14. Switch the active version, and roll back

questions.text: What counts as a candidate 'timeout' in the worker? Is there a deadline like the API's 125 ms, and does a candidate result slower than 80 ms count as an error or only show up in the p99 latency?
How often is the popular list refreshed into each instance, and where do instances read it from (the daily table or object)? Does a refresh run on a background thread like the config poll?

answers.text: Rollback swaps the two fields: active becomes the old previous, and previous becomes the version just rolled back from. Both stay resident on every instance and both stay in the materialization union, so running the command again rolls forward, and a second rollback does not leave previous pointing at the active version. This is the simplest option that keeps the one-minute rollback working in both directions. Added to step 14.

The worker uses the same 125 ms inference deadline as the API. A model error or a miss of that deadline is a candidate error. A result slower than 80 ms but within 125 ms is not an error: it only counts in the p99 latency, where the 80 ms gate applies. A timed-out attempt is recorded with a latency of 125 ms. Reason: the candidate must be judged under the conditions it would face as the active model. Added to step 10.

Each instance refreshes the popular list from the daily table or object on its own background thread, like the config poll, so no request waits on it. I proposed every 10 minutes because the list only changes daily, so the lag is harmless. The brief gives no interval, so this is a proposal. Added to step 4 and as open item 10.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one request for user U through the system, then cover how a model gets released.

1. **Request arrives.** `GET /recommendations?user_id=U` hits one API instance. The instance checks `user_id`. If it is invalid, it returns 400. It starts a 150 ms deadline and reads its in-memory copy of the routing config. That config is `{active, previous, shadow}`. It also takes a reference to the active model, so a pointer swap mid-request can't change the model under it. It computes `bucket = hash(salt + user_id) mod 100`. U is in shadow if a candidate is set and `bucket < shadow.percent`. The API never loads or runs the candidate. An instance takes traffic only after it has read the config and loaded the active and previous models. If that fails at cold start, it takes no traffic.

2. **Feature lookup (30 ms).** The API does one key-value read in the online feature store, keyed by U. The read returns one record: `features{}` plus `materialized_at`. The record holds features for the active, previous and candidate versions. The API checks freshness itself (`now - materialized_at > 6h`) and does not rely on a TTL. The request becomes a fallback if any of these is true. The lookup times out (`timeout`). There is no record (`no_features`). The record is stale (`stale`). A feature the active version requires is missing (`missing_feature`). The model is not called in those cases.

3. **Active model inference.** The model is in the API process's memory. It reads only the features named in its registry entry. It returns scored item IDs. The API removes duplicates, applies filters and keeps the top 20. If fewer than 20 remain, it tops up from the in-memory popular list, skipping items already present. That response is still `fallback: false`, and the topped-up count is recorded. If nothing remains, that counts as an inference failure. The response is `{items, fallback:false, model_version:N}`. The API checks the remaining time before and after inference. Missing the 125 ms hard deadline is a failure. Any inference error or missed deadline goes to step 4 and is counted against the active version.

4. **Fallback.** On any failure in step 2 or 3, the API returns the popular list with `fallback: true` and a `reason` (`timeout`, `no_features`, `stale`, `missing_feature` or `inference_error`). The list is one global list, recomputed daily. Each instance holds a copy in memory. A background thread refreshes it from the daily table or object, proposed every 10 minutes. If a refresh fails, the instance keeps the last good list. An instance can't start without a list. This path does no network I/O. Alerts watch the fallback rate, the mix of reasons and the age of the popular list.

5. **Shadow handoff after the response.** This happens only if U is in the shadow bucket and the response came from step 3. Fallback responses are never shadowed. The response is written to the caller first. Then the API puts one message on a bounded, non-blocking in-process buffer. The message holds the request ID, time, user ID, the feature record, the active version, and the active output (items and latency). A background thread ships the buffer to a message queue in small batches. The enqueue never waits or retries on the request thread. If the buffer is full or the queue is down, the message is dropped and a counter goes up. No exception reaches the response. The API does not check whether the candidate's features exist. The worker handles that.

6. **Shadow worker (separate service).** The worker consumes a queue message and reads the routing config, which it may cache for a few seconds. If `shadow` is null, it discards the message. If it doesn't hold the candidate, it loads it from the registry, keeping one candidate resident, and messages wait meanwhile. It checks that the snapshot has every feature the candidate requires. It also checks that the record age (request time minus `materialized_at`) was under 6 hours. If either check fails, it records a skip (`missing_feature` or `stale`) and does not run the model. This is what guarantees a candidate never runs on features the store lacks. Otherwise it runs inference with the same code, hardware class and 125 ms deadline as the API, and measures latency. It writes a row to the results store. The row has the request ID, user ID, `shadow_salt`, candidate and active versions, both item lists, candidate latency, error, skip reason and feature age. A model error or deadline miss is a candidate error, recorded with 125 ms latency. A worker crash or lost message is counted as loss, not as a candidate error. Nothing on the request path reads these rows.

7. **Hourly materialization.** This feeds step 2. An hourly job reads a warehouse snapshot and writes one record per user to the online store. `materialized_at` is the snapshot time. It writes the union of features required by the active, previous and candidate versions. It rebuilds that union from the current routing config on every run. A candidate counts as soon as it is set, even at `percent: 0`. If the job fails, nothing is rolled back and the store keeps its old records. Users fall back with `stale` once records pass 6 hours. Writes are per record, so a half-finished run leaves a safe mix of old and new records. There is an alert after 2 missed runs and a page at about 4 hours since the last success.

8. **Registering a version.** The training pipeline stores a model as a new numbered, immutable version in the model registry, with its list of required feature names. A version with an incomplete registration has no `registered` status and can't be selected.

9. **Delivering config changes and models without a redeploy.** Each instance polls the registry every 10 seconds on a background thread. If `active` or `previous` names a version it doesn't hold, it loads that version in the background while requests keep using the current model. It swaps the in-memory pointer atomically only after a successful load. It keeps exactly the active and previous versions resident, and drops others once no request holds them. It never preloads a shadow candidate. It reports its loaded version in health metrics. If the registry is unreachable, the instance keeps its last config and keeps serving. If a load fails, it keeps the current version and alerts. Instances may briefly disagree on the version, and each response states its `model_version`.

10. **Starting shadow for a candidate.** Someone asks the promotion tool to shadow a registered version.
    - The tool first checks that no other candidate is in shadow.
    - Phase 1 writes `shadow:{candidate, percent:0, salt}`. The next materialization run then includes the candidate's features. After that run, the tool samples user records and reports, per required feature, the share of records that have it.
    - Phase 2 repeats the feature check. A feature present in no sampled record blocks the step. A partial share does not block. If the check passes, it writes `percent:10` with a new salt and records the write time as the start of the shadow run.
    - The 7-day clock starts at that time. A restart gets a new salt and start time, and the clock begins again.

11. **Gate report.** The evaluation job runs hourly over the results store. It counts only rows whose `shadow_salt` matches the current run. It computes the candidate error rate (errors divided by attempts, skips excluded), the p99 candidate latency, and the days since the run start. It also computes the skip and drop rates, plus comparisons with the active model (overlap@20, rank correlation, empty or short list share, catalogue coverage). It writes a new timestamped report with an ID to the registry. If the job is down, the report goes stale. If the results are incomplete, the report shows the gap and the gate stays closed.

12. **Promotion gate.** Someone asks the promotion tool to activate the candidate. It refuses and lists what's unmet unless all of these hold:
    - at least 7 days in shadow;
    - error rate under 0.5%;
    - p99 latency under 80 ms;
    - the latest report is no older than 24 hours and meets those numbers;
    - the ML lead has approved this exact version against a report no older than 24 hours;
    - a fresh feature check passes.
    The approval record holds the person, time, version and report ID.

13. **Switch and rollback.**
    - Promotion: the tool writes `previous = old active`, `active = candidate`, `shadow = null`. Instances load the new version in the background on their next poll (step 9) and switch when the load finishes. The tool reads health metrics and prints how many instances are on the new version. Promotion is complete when every ready instance reports it. Any instance not there after 5 minutes is listed for a human. The tool takes no automatic action.
    - Rollback: one command swaps `active` and `previous`. No approval is needed. It takes effect within one poll (10 s) plus pointer swap time. Both versions are already resident and both stay in the materialization union.
    - Kill switch: it sets `shadow` to null. API instances stop sending within one poll, and workers discard leftover messages.
    - Whether A/B testing sits between shadow and the switch is undecided. Product has to choose.
gaps: Which instance serves a request and how requests are distributed to instances (load balancing, how many instances) is not stated, so I can't say how the caller reaches an instance.

How the in-memory routing config gets refreshed in the request-time read is described (10 s poll), but how a promotion tool or command physically writes to the registry (interface, atomicity, how concurrent writers such as the evaluation job and a person are serialised) is not described.
The document says the evaluation job is one of the routing config writers, but never says when or why it writes the config (for example, whether it ever changes `shadow`). I can't explain that step.

Where candidate item IDs come from (the whole catalogue or an earlier retrieval step) and the exact filter rules are not specified, so I can't explain what the model actually scores or how filtering decides what is removed.

How the shadow worker receives or knows which messages belong to the current shadow run, other than comparing the config. It is unclear whether a message carries the salt. The result row has `shadow_salt`, but the document doesn't say where the worker gets it (presumably from the config it reads).

How the approval by the ML lead is recorded through tooling (which command or interface), and how the tool verifies the approver's identity, is not specified. Authentication is left to the platform team.

The mechanism by which the evaluation job turns the message and results store into 'inference attempts' and 'loss' counts. This includes how loss is measured against the number of messages sent, given that drops happen in the API and queue and worker losses are invisible to the results store. It is not stated.
How instance health metrics are collected and read by the promotion tool is not given (where they are kept is listed as unspecified).
